Maladaptive Strategies.value: I push myself to exercise excessively

Negative Appraisals.value: I have lost my faith in people, life, or a higher power
I feel that others can see what happened to me just by looking at me
Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore

issues.item: Avoid Perpetrator Cues: Anything that reminds me of the person who harmed me
issues.explanation: The trauma type is trauma to a loved one, but this maladaptive strategy presumes a direct perpetrator who harmed the patient. That is hard to reconcile unless the loved one's trauma also directly involved interpersonal harm to the patient, which is not indicated here.

issues.item: Humiliation: I feel permanently humiliated by what happened
issues.explanation: Permanent humiliation is more characteristic of direct interpersonal victimization. With a loved-one trauma, this appraisal is not impossible, but in combination with 'others can see what happened to me' it implies a self-referential shame exposure theme that fits poorly unless the patient was also directly victimized.

vignette: Nalani's eyes still wandered to the spot where her daughter had lain in the hospital bed, the beeping of machines and antiseptic smell an unbearable reminder of those fateful days. It was a year ago that her world crumbled when her daughter, Leilani, was involved in a tragic accident. The sound of incomprehensible chatter, like the murmurs of the medical staff discussing her daughter's condition, still sent Nalani's mind racing back to that ICU room. Even physical locations – hospitals, clinics, or any place with a similar layout – triggered an overwhelming sense of dread. To cope, Nalani had started avoiding friends and social gatherings, fearful of being asked about Leilani or having to relive the memories. She would also excessively exercise, pushing her body to its limits as if trying to outrun the pain. These habits had become a double-edged sword: while they provided temporary relief, they also reinforced her negative appraisals – she felt lost and disconnected from the world, questioning the very fabric of life and her faith in people. The thought that others could see what happened to Leilani just by looking at her tormented Nalani, making her withdraw further into isolation. As time passed, Nalani's maladaptive strategies only intensified. She would avoid hospitals and medical cues, going so far as to refuse check-ups for herself, fearing that any interaction with the healthcare system would unravel her fragile emotional state. Her excessive exercise had taken a toll on her body, but she couldn't seem to stop – it was as if she needed to punish herself for not being able to protect Leilani. This self-destructive cycle further entrenched her negative appraisals: nothing in life felt meaningful anymore; even her work as an architect, once a source of pride and joy, now seemed hollow. The loss of faith in people, life, and a higher power had become a perpetual shroud over Nalani's existence. She couldn't shake the feeling that she was living in a world devoid of purpose or meaning. Her excessive exercise and avoidance behaviors had not only affected her relationships but also impacted her job performance – projects were lagging, and clients were growing concerned about her reliability. The weight of these negative appraisals continued to fuel Nalani's maladaptive strategies. She became trapped in a cycle where the triggers reminded her of Leilani's accident, leading to avoidance behaviors that, in turn, strengthened her negative beliefs about the world. This loop was suffocating her – she felt like she was drowning in a sea of despair. It wasn't until Nalani received an ultimatum from her employer, threatening to terminate her contract due to her declining performance, that she realized she needed help. The threat of losing everything she had worked for – the one thing that still connected her to Leilani's memory – finally brought Nalani to seek professional help. As she sat in the therapist's office, surrounded by unfamiliar yet comforting surroundings, she knew she was taking a tentative step toward breaking free from the cycle that had consumed her life.
